title: Sensitivity or Criterion? Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act

paper.title: Sensitivity or Criterion? Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act
paper.abstract:
Abstract Before an agent acts it must decide whether any action is warranted. Benchmarks that ask this question
report one accuracy, which cannot distinguish a model that fails to recognize a warranted action from one
that recognizes it but is reluctant to act. Signal-detection theory separates the two as sensitivity and
criterion, but a criterion estimated from authored binary labels depends on each benchmark’s mix of
examples and cannot be compared across benchmarks. We introduce FlipAct , a diagnostic
built on a qualitative representation of what tools do to physical states. A rule over annotated tool
properties computes each question’s answer and a graded evidence score, with the Yes/No boundary fixed
at zero for every model, so every answer is computed, not written by a model. Questions are built from 2 × 2 2\times 2 quads that hold the required
knowledge fixed while the state flips. The slope of a model’s Yes-rate against the score is its
sensitivity, and the score where it crosses one half is its criterion. Across 44 44 open models, sensitivity rises
with size within a family, and its ranking agrees with three of four external when-to-act
benchmarks. Models respond to the sign of the evidence rather than its size, accepting actions that
leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, most models are conservative and stay so when the question is
rephrased. In some models this is a preference for answering No, and the criterion is not set by size. Activation
steering moves the criterion with the weights fixed, and distilling a model from its own steered copy
moves it in the weights, without a significant change in sensitivity. The distilled shift carries to six
external benchmarks with sensitivity kept, including two without a Yes/No answer. Accuracy rises where
the model started conservative and falls where it started permissive.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language model (LLM) agents must decide whether to act before they decide how. Benchmarks for agents mostly score the action once taken: whether the chosen function, its arguments and the trajectory are correct ( Patil et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2026 ) . Those that study the decision itself, in tool calling ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , clarification ( Li et al., 2026 ) and abstention ( Kirichenko et al., 2026 ) , report a single accuracy, and that number mixes two ways to fail. A model may not recognize whether a situation warrants action, a failure of its sensitivity ; or it may recognize the situation and still be too reluctant or too ready to act, a failure of its criterion . Too conservative a criterion refuses benign requests ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) or answers from memory where a tool was needed; too permissive a criterion acts where nothing warrants it. On When2Call ( Ross et al., 2025 ) , gemma-2-9b and Phi-3.5-mini reach balanced accuracies of 0.65 0.65 and 0.64 0.64 with opposite behavior: the first rarely calls the tool, even where it should, and the second calls it on most examples, many where it should not (Figure 1 a). They separate the two kinds of example about equally well, so on this benchmark the first should act more and the second less. Signal-detection theory ( Green et al., 1966 ) separates sensitivity ( d ′ d^{\prime} ) from criterion (Figure 1 b; § 3.1 ), but on a benchmark with binary labels the criterion it recovers is relative to that benchmark’s mix of examples, and no zero is shared across benchmarks. Comparing criteria needs a fixed boundary on a common evidence scale, which authored binary labels do not provide ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 , cf.) . 0 0.5 1 call rate .40 .10 .86 .58 gemma-2-9b bal. acc. .65 Phi-3.5-mini bal. acc. .64 should call should not (a) Same accuracy, opposite calls unwarranted warranted Phi-3.5-mini’s criterion gemma-2-9b’s criterion evidence for acting → \rightarrow same d ′ d^{\prime} (b) Same d ′ d^{\prime} , two criteria No ( Δ ​ U ≤ 0 \Delta U\leq 0 ) Yes ( Δ ​ U > 0 \Delta U>0 ) Δ ​ U \Delta U − 3 -3 − 2 -2 − 1 -1 0 0 1 1 2 2 3 3 dehumid. dry humid. wet humid. dry dehumid. wet (c) Evidence computed by rule Figure 1: (a) Share of should-call and of should-not-call When2Call examples that each model calls. (b) Schematic: at one sensitivity d ′ d^{\prime} , the two models’ criteria trade hits for false alarms at the same accuracy. (c) The quad of Figure 2 on the evidence scale Δ ​ U \Delta U that FlipAct computes by rule, with the Yes/No boundary fixed at zero. FlipAct supplies such a scale by computing the evidence for acting. Its design draws on qualitative process theory ( Forbus, 1984 ) , which describes physical change by the sign of each quantity’s change and a coarse ordinal magnitude, enough to say what an action does to a state without numbers. Each question shows a situation and a candidate tool and asks whether using the tool is warranted. The state and the tool each have a sign and an ordinal magnitude on a physical axis. A rule over these properties computes the evidence score Δ ​ U \Delta U , how much closer the action brings the state to its goal, with the Yes/No boundary at zero (Figure 1 c). The design unit is a 2 × 2 2\times 2 quad : two tools, each shown in the state it fixes and in the state it worsens, so the knowledge needed to answer stays the same and the state decides the answer (Figure 2 ). Fitting a model’s Yes-rate against Δ ​ U \Delta U gives its sensitivity as the slope a a and its criterion as the score τ \tau where it crosses one half. Across 44 44 open models (§ 4 ), sensitivity behaves as expected of a capability: it rises with size inside a family, and its ranking agrees with external d ′ d^{\prime} on three of four when-to-act benchmarks. Models read the sign of the evidence rather than its size, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, the criterion is mostly conservative, in some models through a preference for answering No. It is a stable per-model setting, not set by size: two releases of Mistral-Small-24B sit on opposite sides of zero. We move the criterion separately from sensitivity in two ways (§ 5 ). At inference, adding a direction read from the model’s own activations ( Zou et al., 2023 ; Turner et al., 2023 ; Ke et al., 2026 ) shifts the criterion with the weights fixed. In the weights, distilling the model from its own steered copy shifts the criterion on four models from three developers with no significant change in sensitivity, and a random direction of the same norm does not. The shift carries beyond FlipAct ’s Yes/No format: on benchmarks without a Yes/No answer it exceeds the shift from a teacher that only favors Yes, on both models tested. On every benchmark, accuracy rises or falls as the starting criterion predicts. Supervised training on the computed labels instead raises sensitivity and moves the criterion with it.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: 1. A measurement scheme that splits when-to-act accuracy into a sensitivity and a criterion, read against an evidence scale computed by rule with the Yes/No boundary fixed for every model. 2. FlipAct , built by an automated pipeline in which language models only annotate what a tool does, while the states and every answer follow from the rule. 3. Evidence that the criterion moves separately from sensitivity: steering and distillation from a steered copy move the criterion, while training on the computed labels raises sensitivity.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: When-to-act evaluation. Benchmarks for deciding whether to act cover tool calling ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2025 ) , clarification ( Li et al., 2026 ) , abstention ( Kirichenko et al., 2026 ) and over-refusal ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Most share three design choices: ground truth is authored by humans or an LLM judge, the evidence for acting is a binary label, and performance is a single rate that conflates a model’s sensitivity with its criterion. Li et al. (2026) instead compute ground truth by constraint satisfaction, and Sun et al. (2026) fix a controlled call/no-call boundary with deliberate no-tool cases. Neither flips a world-state while holding the required knowledge fixed, and none of these benchmarks grades the evidence for acting per question. We reuse four of them as external tests (§ 4.2 ) and measure transfer on six benchmarks (§ 5.3 ). App. F compares twelve on these design choices. Signal detection and language models. Signal-detection theory separates an observer’s sensitivity from its criterion ( Green et al., 1966 ) . Reading a benchmark score as the measurement of a latent quantity raises the question of whether it measures what it is read as ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 ; Bean et al., 2026 ) . Cacioli (2026) fits signal-detection models to factual question answering with the model’s answer log-probability as evidence, so the criterion sits on each model’s own confidence scale. Shi et al. (2026) read a call/no-call offset off sparse-autoencoder features on When2Call and cancel it by steering. Their offset is an intercept on an internal margin, compared within one model and without a separate sensitivity. FlipAct places the criterion on a rule-computed evidence scale shared across questions and models, estimates it separately from sensitivity with the required knowledge held fixed, and moves it into the weights.

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries: signal detection
sections.text: Signal-detection theory ( Green et al., 1966 ) models an observer who reports a signal whenever a scalar amount of evidence exceeds a threshold. The sensitivity d ′ d^{\prime} is the distance between the evidence distributions of signal and noise trials in units of their spread, and the criterion c c is where the threshold sits relative to their midpoint. From the hit rate H H and the false-alarm rate FA \mathrm{FA} the equal-variance estimators, with z z the inverse of the standard normal distribution function, are d ′ = z ⁡ ( H ) − z ⁡ ( FA ) , c = − 1 2 ​ ( z ⁡ ( H ) + z ⁡ ( FA ) ) . d^{\prime}\;=\;z(H)-z(\mathrm{FA}),\qquad c\;=\;-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(z(H)+z(\mathrm{FA})\bigr). (1) In when-to-act terms a hit is acting when one should and a false alarm is acting when one should not. A positive c c is conservative. FlipAct supplies an evidence score per question, and the same two quantities become the slope a a and the crossing point τ \tau of a model’s Yes-rate against that score (§ 4.1 ). Every comparison in the paper pairs a a with d ′ d^{\prime} and τ \tau with c c . An interactive version is online. 1 1 1 https://sixundong.com/projects/flipact

sections.heading: 3.2 Same knowledge, flipped state
sections.text: Template Situation: The <object> is <state> . [ <supply> ] The goal is to bring the <object> back to a normal state. Action: a person uses a <tool> . Is using the <tool> a wise choice in this situation? Answer Yes or No. One quad , object room humidifier industrial dehumidifier wets by 2 dries by 3 very dry Yes + 2 +2 No − 3 -3 dangerously wet No − 2 -2 Yes + 3 +3 Figure 2: The question template (left) and one quad (right) with each question’s answer and evidence score Δ ​ U \Delta U . The slot [<supply>] states that a prerequisite is met, for tools that have one. Each question shows a physical situation, the goal of returning it to normal and one candidate tool, and asks whether using the tool is a wise choice. All questions share one minimal template (Figure 2 ), as do the stimuli of template-based diagnostics ( McCoy et al., 2019 ; Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) , so only the tool, the state and their outcome vary. Physical situations are used because a tool’s effect on a state can be written as an explicit qualitative transition: a humidifier helps a dry room and harms a wet one. In the quad of Figure 2 , a humidifier that adds two steps of moisture and an industrial dehumidifier that removes three are crossed with a very dry and a dangerously wet room. Every question of the quad needs the same two facts, what the tool does and what the room needs. For a given tool only the state changes, and with it the answer, so a model that knows what a humidifier is for must still read the state. Quads and state flips are controls built into the set. The main set has 1,880 1{,}880 questions: 840 840 lie in a complete quad and 1,256 1{,}256 belong to a state flip , the same tool with opposite answers in two states. A state flip separates a model that ignores the state, which gives both questions about the same Yes–No logit margin, from one that is merely permissive, which may answer Yes to both but still ranks the warranted one higher (App. D.3 , D.7 ). Every situation has as many Yes as No questions, so the description of the world does not predict the answer.

sections.heading: 3.3 Ground truth and evidence by rule
sections.text: Each situation fixes an integer state v v on a physical axis (thermal transfer, moisture, mechanical cohesion, …) with the goal at 0 0 . Each tool carries a direction δ ∈ { + 1 , − 1 } \delta\in\{+1,-1\} and an ordinal magnitude band μ ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 } \mu\in\{1,2,3\} on that axis ( Forbus, 1984 , in qualitative process theory, a sign and a place in a quantity space;) , optionally conditional on a prerequisite. Applying it moves the state to v + δ ​ μ v+\delta\mu , and the process behind that change is not modeled. The evidence score is the utility of the action, how much closer to the goal it leaves the world, Δ ​ U = | v | − | v + δ ​ μ | , Yes ⇔ Δ ​ U > 0 , \Delta U\;=\;|v|\;-\;|v+\delta\mu|,\qquad\texttt{Yes}\iff\Delta U>0, and a tool with unmet prerequisites carries Δ ​ U = − 2 \Delta U=-2 for each, a value set by convention. The question type follows from the same computation: a wrong-direction tool is destructive , a right-direction tool that overshoots or acts on a state already at the goal is redundant , and a tool applied without its prerequisite is prerequisite . Because v v and μ \mu are integers, Δ ​ U \Delta U takes seven values on [ − 3 , 3 ] [-3,3] . A question conveys | v | |v| only by the adverb slightly , very or dangerously , and μ \mu only by the tool itself. Language models annotate each tool’s axis, direction, magnitude and prerequisite, and the rule computes the answer from those properties.

sections.heading: 3.4 An automated build
sections.text: FlipAct is generated by a pipeline (Figure 3 ) that needs no per-question human annotation or adjudication. Its specification is written once: the physical axes, a closed vocabulary of tool properties, the rule of § 3.3 and the template. Ten lexical, medical and visually grounded resources supply 149,840 149{,}840 candidate entities, and two annotator models, Qwen3.5-27B and gemma-4-31b, fill the vocabulary for each. Where they disagree, both arbitrate against the specification, and unresolved records are dropped. Tool records (one tool, one axis) are paired when they act in opposite directions on that axis and target object, and states, answers, question types and text follow by rule. A balance selection keeps 1,880 1{,}880 of the 6,176 6{,}176 rendered questions. Two matched-pair supplementary sets, 342 342 already-satisfied and 224 224 prerequisite-blocked questions, are kept outside the fits. A new axis, a new tool inventory or a larger set runs through the same steps at the cost of annotator calls (App. A ). Entity pool 149,840 149{,}840 entities Tool-property annotation 2,876 2{,}876 records Screens: axis, use, magnitude, deployability 1,638 1{,}638 tool records Pairing 1,422 1{,}422 tool pairs Situation synthesis states by rule Answer and Δ ​ U \Delta U by rule 0 0 LLM calls Template rendering 6,176 6{,}176 questions Balance selection 1,880 1{,}880 questions tool records questions Figure 3: The FlipAct construction pipeline. Language models are used only in the orange steps, which annotate and screen tool properties; answers and evidence scores are computed by rule. A lexical probe trained on the question text is at chance on held-out situations whose tools it has not seen (App. A.5 ), and recomputing the ground truth independently of the build gives zero mismatches. A model’s judgment enters only where tools are annotated and screened, and a model family outside the build reproduces every tool/non-tool judgment, nine in ten axis judgments and every magnitude band to within one band, two in three exactly. Perturbing the annotations at that rate, or until a quarter of the computed answers change, keeps the rankings by a a and τ \tau intact and moves criteria toward acting, so it cannot produce the conservative criteria (App. A.6 ).

sections.heading: 4 Measuring sensitivity and criterion
sections.text: Models. To see how the coordinates a a and τ \tau vary with size and family, we fit 44 44 open models, all but five with reasoning off (App. B.7 ), from 0.6 0.6 B to 70 70 B parameters and fifteen families, among them Qwen3 and Qwen3.5, Gemma 2–4, Llama 3, Mistral and Phi (App. Tables 9 – 10 ). External benchmarks. To test whether the coordinates capture what when-to-act benchmarks score, we compare them with four, each posing the decision in a different domain. Every example is one where acting is right or one where withholding is, and d ′ d^{\prime} and c c follow from Eq. 1 with acting as the response. On BFCL acting is calling a listed function, which is right when one fits the query; on When2Call it is choosing the tool call among four replies (call, ask, cannot answer, answer directly); QuestBench and When2Tool ask Yes/No whether the model already has enough information to answer and whether it would need a tool (App. Table 11 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 The fit and the response profile
sections.text: On FlipAct every question carries a computed evidence score, so we fit the model’s Yes-rate as a logistic curve over that score ( Green et al., 1966 ) : P ⁡ ( Yes ∣ Δ ​ U ) = σ ⁡ ( a ⁡ ( Δ ​ U − τ ) ) . P(\text{Yes}\mid\Delta U)\;=\;\sigma\!\bigl(a\,(\Delta U-\tau)\bigr). (2) Here σ \sigma is the logistic function, the slope a a the sensitivity and the crossing point τ \tau the criterion. A positive τ \tau means the fitted curve crosses one half above the rule’s boundary, so the model answers Yes less often than the rule warrants, which we call conservative. A criterion is estimable when a ≥ 0.15 a\geq 0.15 and SE ⁡ ( τ ) ≤ 2.0 \mathrm{SE}(\tau)\leq 2.0 , and well determined when it also lies inside the score range; beyond ± 3 \pm 3 it is reported as a bound. Both coordinates have split-half reliability above 0.9 0.9 (App. B.2 ). On external benchmarks we use d ′ d^{\prime} and c c (Eq. 1 ); a model readier to act has lower τ \tau and c c . Figure 4: Yes-rate at each evidence score for the 21 21 reasoning-off models with a well-determined criterion (gray), with their median and interquartile band. Response profile. Models read the sign of the evidence, not its size (Figure 4 ). Yes-rates jump between Δ ​ U = − 1 \Delta U=-1 and 0 0 , significantly in 19 19 of the 21 21 reasoning-off models with a well-determined criterion, and are flat on either side: no model answers Yes reliably more often at Δ ​ U = + 3 \Delta U=+3 than at + 1 +1 . The step sits one unit below the rule’s boundary: models accept actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. The questions at Δ ​ U = 0 \Delta U=0 are all redundant slight overshoots, so this set cannot tell whether that placement belongs to the models or to the rule. Models do withhold when the state is already at its goal or a prerequisite is unmet (App. B.2 ), so the overshoot is the one redundancy they accept. The sign of τ \tau is set by the height of the Yes plateau, not by the step: for the median model the Yes-rate on helpful actions stays near one half (Figure 4 ). Reading τ \tau . A step function at the sign of the evidence predicts held-out answers as well as the logistic. Still, τ \tau tracks the criterion divided by sensitivity: with c / d ′ c/d^{\prime} of Eq. 1 read from hits on Δ ​ U > 0 \Delta U>0 and false alarms on Δ ​ U < 0 \Delta U<0 , τ ≈ − 0.09 + 3.22 ​ c / d ′ \tau\approx-0.09+3.22\,c/d^{\prime} ( r = 0.999 r=0.999 ), and both find the same models conservative (App. B.2 – B.3 ). In 9 9 of the 21 21 models the Yes-rate never reaches one half, so τ \tau is where the fitted curve, not the data, crosses it. We therefore read τ \tau by sign and rank.

sections.heading: 4.2 Sensitivity grows with size and agrees with external benchmarks
sections.text: Within a family, a a rises with size: Qwen3 goes from 0.34 0.34 at 4B to 0.58 0.58 at 32B, and the one exception is Qwen3.5, which peaks at 9B. Twelve models fit below 0.30 0.30 , among them widely deployed small instruct models, and their Yes-rates span almost the whole range: a model can be permissive or conservative about a tool and still be unable to tell when using it is warranted (Figure 5 ). Figure 5: Sensitivity against criterion for the 27 27 reasoning-off models with an estimable criterion, with the distribution of the well-determined criteria on the right. Hollow markers at the edges are criteria beyond ± 3 \pm 3 . The line joins the two same-size Mistral-Small-24B releases. FlipAct sensitivity predicts external d ′ d^{\prime} on three of the four benchmarks (Figure 6 a). The comparison uses a panel : of the 39 39 reasoning-off models, 27 27 have an estimable criterion and 21 21 a well-determined one, and the 18 18 of these with a ≥ 0.30 a\geq 0.30 and usable external d ′ d^{\prime} and c c form the panel, so that both sides of each comparison are estimated reliably (App. B.4 varies the cutoff on a a ). All three relations hold with model size partialed out (App. B.5 ). This agreement across three domains and formats supports reading a a as the sensitivity these benchmarks score. On When2Tool the relation is not significant. Figure 6: (a) Correlation across the panel between FlipAct sensitivity a a and external d ′ d^{\prime} , with bootstrap intervals; the hollow point is not significant. (b) Criterion against model size for the families with three or more estimable members, one line per generation. Hollow markers with an arrow are criteria beyond + 3 +3 .

sections.heading: 4.3 Criterion: a per-model setting, conservative by default
sections.text: Eighteen of the 21 21 reasoning-off models with a well-determined criterion are positive on the canonical wording of Figure 2 : they answer Yes less often than the rule warrants (Figure 5 ), and nearly all tested stay positive under five rephrasings (App. C ). The criterion is one setting across question types: models that accept more destructive actions also accept more slight overshoots on other questions ( ρ = 0.88 \rho=0.88 , 27 27 models, a ≥ 0.30 a\geq 0.30 ), though most accept overshoots more readily. As in signal detection, the criterion collects every bias in the response, including a preference for one answer word. We also ask each question in three reversed wordings, such as “Is using the tool a mistake?”, under which No means act. After recoding, a preference for No raises the canonical criterion and lowers the reversed one, so writing them as τ d + b \tau_{d}+b and τ d − b \tau_{d}-b separates a threshold on the evidence, τ d \tau_{d} , from the preference, b b (App. C ). For the three Qwen3.5 models and GLM-4-32B, b b is + 3 +3 to + 4 +4 and τ d \tau_{d} within a unit of zero; the other twelve of the 16 16 models tested stay conservative without it. JEV ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ) , a model that returns a probability, not text, and so has no answer word to prefer, is conservative too and steps at the sign of the evidence (App. E ). Where the criterion sits is a property of the model more than of its size. The two Mistral-Small-24B releases are the same size and land on opposite sides of zero, at + 2.18 +2.18 (2501) and − 1.10 -1.10 (3.2, 2506) (Figure 5 ). Inside a family τ \tau drifts toward zero as models grow, in Qwen3, in the dense Qwen3.5 models and across the Gemma generations (Figure 6 b). Part of this drift follows from rising sensitivity, since τ \tau tracks the criterion divided by sensitivity. Families differ in their typical τ \tau , so pooled over all models the relation with size vanishes. The criterion measured on FlipAct does not consistently predict a model’s c c on other benchmarks: across the panel the correlation is near zero on When2Call (Pearson r = − 0.01 r=-0.01 ), QuestBench and When2Tool, and positive on BFCL ( r = + 0.51 r=+0.51 ), where it rests on the three models with the lowest τ \tau (App. Table 15 ). Section 5.3 asks instead whether moving τ \tau moves c c .

sections.heading: 5 Moving the criterion
sections.text: We ask whether the criterion can be moved while sensitivity stays fixed, at inference (§ 5.1 ) and in the weights (§ 5.2 ), and whether the moved criterion carries to external benchmarks (§ 5.3 ). Such a move trades misses for false alarms and cannot raise accuracy beyond what sensitivity allows.

We steer five open models, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-27B, gemma-2-9b, Mistral-Small-24B (the 2501 release, Mistral-24B below) and phi-4, and measure the effect on When2Call ( Ross et al., 2025 ) , on 600 600 examples, half call and half withhold (eleven more models in App. D.1 ). Method. Steering follows the standard recipe ( Turner et al., 2023 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Arditi et al., 2024 ) . A logistic probe from the final-token residual stream at relative depth 0.6 0.6 to the model’s own Yes/No answers on the FlipAct questions gives the criterion direction w ^ \hat{w} , which is added during generation to the residual-stream activation h h at that layer as h ← h + λ ​ w ^ h\leftarrow h+\lambda\hat{w} . For each model the strength λ ⋆ \lambda^{\star} is the one with the lowest When2Call criterion among those that keep d ′ d^{\prime} within 25 % 25\% of its unsteered value. Results. The direction moves the When2Call criterion toward acting on all five models (Table 1 ). On Qwen3-8B, gemma-2-9b and Mistral-24B the shift is at least three times that of same-norm random and orthogonal directions and keeps over two thirds of its size when the refusal, sycophancy and engagement directions are projected out of w ^ \hat{w} ; over sixteen models, eleven move significantly toward acting and four pass both controls (App. D.1 ). The shift is small on Qwen3.5-27B, which starts near zero on When2Call and whose FlipAct criterion is mostly a preference for No, and there it does not exceed random directions of the same norm. On phi-4, which starts permissive and moves least, it does not hold when the strength is chosen on one half of the examples and measured on the other (App. D.1 ). On four models steering gains hits at the cost of correct withholds, and on all five, accuracy changes by at most four points. With the direction fit on one half of FlipAct and measured on the other, it also moves the criterion of Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-27B toward zero and raises their accuracy by 2.6 2.6 and 1.6 1.6 points.

sections.heading: 5.2 Distilling from a steered copy puts the criterion into the weights
sections.text: Models and data. As an existence proof that the criterion can be placed in the weights, we distill four students from three developers, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, gemma-3-12b and Mistral-24B, each from its own steered copy. The FlipAct main set is split in half so that no situation or tool record appears on both sides. Students train on one half ( 940 940 questions) with three seeds per condition, and every result is measured on the held-out half, so baselines differ from the full-set values of § 4 . sections.heading: 5.3 The distilled criterion moves the same way on six external benchmarks
sections.text: Benchmarks. To test whether the shift generalizes beyond FlipAct ’s physical questions and its Yes/No format, each student is tested on six unseen benchmarks, scored with d ′ d^{\prime} and c c . Four ask whether to act now: When2Call and When2Tool ( Sun et al., 2026 ) (call a tool), QuestBench ( Li et al., 2026 ) (ask or solve) and BFCL-miss-func ( Patil et al., 2025 ) (the needed function is removed from the list). Two ask a planning judgment: ACPBench ( Kokel et al., 2025 ) (does an action apply) and CaT-Bench ( Lal et al., 2024 ) (must one step precede another). When2Call offers four replies, BFCL-miss-func takes a free-form call or refusal, and the other four take Yes or No. Figure 7: Criterion shift on six external benchmarks after criterion distillation (filled) and under the random-direction control (hollow), seed means ± \pm SD. Moving the FlipAct criterion moves c c the same way on every benchmark, although across models it does not consistently predict a benchmark’s c c (§ 4.3 ). On all 23 23 scored model–benchmark pairs, c c moves toward acting in every seed, and every control moves less than the distilled student beside it (Figure 7 ). Sensitivity is kept: the criterion-free AUC from answer log-probabilities, available on five benchmarks, stays unchanged for every student (Table 4 ). Answer preference. On a Yes/No format a shift toward acting and a shift toward Yes coincide. On FlipAct most of the distilled shift flips sign under the reversed wordings of § 4.3 , so there it shifts the preference for Yes, the form the decision to act takes on a Yes/No format (App. D.5 ). Whether more than that preference carries over shows only where the answer has no Yes: if a Yes preference were all that transfers, a student distilled from a teacher whose Yes logits are raised by a constant tuned to the steered teacher’s Yes-rate would match the criterion-distilled one there. On Qwen3-8B and gemma-3-12b it does not: on When2Call and BFCL-miss-func the criterion-distilled student moves c c further in every seed, though on Qwen3-8B the Yes-bias student reaches half to three quarters of it. On the four Yes/No benchmarks it moves c c as far or further. Accuracy. Accuracy follows the starting point, as a pure criterion shift predicts. Where a student starts conservative, balanced accuracy rises in every case, by up to six points (Table 4 ; all students in App. Table 31 ). Where it starts permissive, accuracy falls by up to four points or stays within its error, except Mistral-24B on When2Tool: its hit rate is already at ceiling, so a shift toward acting only adds false alarms, and accuracy falls about ten points. A criterion shift should thus take its sign from the target benchmark. Steering the five models of § 5.1 toward acting on five benchmarks lowers balanced accuracy on 12 12 of the 25 25 model–benchmark pairs; choosing the sign and strength from fifty labeled examples of each benchmark instead leaves only Mistral-24B on When2Call worse (App. D.6 ). Where the benchmark has an answer token, a scalar bias on that token chosen the same way does as well ( 19 19 of 20 20 pairs), as expected if steering is one offset on the criterion.

sections.heading: 5.4 Labels move sensitivity, and the criterion with it
sections.text: Sensitivity learning , supervised training on the computed labels, tests the converse: whether labels move sensitivity. It uses the same students, split, adapter and seeds, adds 263 263 supplementary questions on the same tool records to the training half, and shuffles the labels within matched groups of questions as its control. It raises a a on every student, by about 0.5 0.5 to 1.2 1.2 , and held-out accuracy by 17 17 to 24 24 points, while the shuffled-label control lowers accuracy (Table 2 ). It also brings τ \tau close to zero, so labels move both coordinates, whereas distillation moves the criterion alone. The gain in sensitivity stays on FlipAct : on the external benchmarks its changes in d ′ d^{\prime} and c c differ in sign across students and are matched by the shuffled-label control. Limitations are discussed in App. G .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We treated the decision to act as a measurement problem. Two models with the same accuracy can need opposite fixes, so a when-to-act benchmark says more when it reports d ′ d^{\prime} and c c beside accuracy. The criterion moves, at inference or in the weights, with a shift whose sign the target benchmark sets, while sensitivity on FlipAct rises with training on labels. On a Yes/No format the criterion also holds a preference between answer words, which reversed wordings separate from the rest.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work evaluates open-weight models on public benchmarks and involves no human subjects. Moving a model’s criterion toward acting makes it act on thinner evidence, a trade-off practitioners should weigh for their application.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: The paper specifies the full experimental setup: the construction of FlipAct and its rule (§ 3 , App. A ), the estimators (§ 4.1 ), and the steering and training procedures with all hyperparameters (§ 5 , App. D.3 ). Every training condition is run with three seeds and reported as the seed mean with its bootstrap error, and every reported change comes with a significance test; steering effects carry bootstrap intervals and are checked on held-out splits. The dataset, code and evaluation logs will be released.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: We used generative AI tools to generate synthetic data sets: in the FlipAct pipeline, language models annotate tool properties (§ 3.4 , App. A ), while every answer and evidence score is computed by rule. We used generative AI tools to implement methods: the evaluation, steering, training and analysis code was written with an AI coding assistant. We also used generative AI tools to aid and polish the writing. We did not use generative AI tools for the other tasks with required disclosure. The authors reviewed all AI-assisted code, data and text and take responsibility for the final content of this work.

sections.heading: Appendix A Construction of FlipAct
sections.text: This section details the construction summarized in § 3 : the annotation schema, the rule that turns a tool into its questions, a worked quad, the build with its counts, and the checks on data quality and on annotation noise.

sections.heading: A.1 Annotation schema
sections.text: Each annotator model (App. A.4 ) fills one record per candidate entity against the closed vocabulary of Table 5 . A value outside the vocabulary is a parse failure and is never mapped to a neighboring value. A tool that acts on two axes becomes one record per axis, and each record carries a single direction. sections.heading: A.2 From a tool to its questions
sections.text: The state of every question is computed from the tool, with the goal at 0 0 . A solution question places the state at v = − δ ​ μ v=-\delta\mu , the deficit the tool closes. A destructive question uses the deficit of the paired tool, which points the other way, so the tool widens the gap. A redundant question uses a deficit of one met by a magnitude of at least two, so the tool crosses the goal and leaves the state no closer. A prerequisite question removes the supply a tool depends on from a solution state. Two tools are paired only when they act on the same axis and target object in opposite directions and differ in magnitude by at most one band, so each tool’s solution state is its partner’s destructive state. A pocket hand warmer pairs with an ice pack on a person, never with an air conditioner in a room. Prerequisite questions and questions whose state is already at the goal are not part of the main set. They go to the two supplementary sets of § 3.4 . Every question is rendered from the template of Figure 2 , with the state adverb slightly , very or dangerously for | v | = 1 , 2 , 3 |v|=1,2,3 . For a tool with a prerequisite, a sentence between the state and the goal reads “The supplies this tool depends on (mains electricity) are available nearby” or “None of the supplies this tool depends on (mains electricity) is available anywhere nearby.” It appears in every question of such a tool, including those whose supply is present, so its presence carries no information about the answer.

sections.heading: A.4 The build
sections.text: Ten lexical, medical and visually grounded resources supply candidate entities: ConceptNet ( Speer et al., 2017 ) , Wikipedia ( Wikipedia contributors, 2026 ) and Wikidata ( Vrandečić and Krötzsch, 2014 ) for breadth; WordNet ( Miller, 1995 ) , LVIS ( Gupta et al., 2019 ) , EPIC-Kitchens ( Damen et al., 2022 ) and AI2-THOR ( Kolve et al., 2017 ) for objects a person handles; MeSH ( Lipscomb, 2000 ) , ChEBI ( Hastings et al., 2016 ) and FrameNet ( Baker et al., 1998 ) for specialist vocabulary. Figure 8 gives the counts at each step. Six filter levels remove duplicate names, abstract suffixes, lemma duplicates, abstract hypernym paths and synonyms, and reclassify domains, leaving 149,840 149{,}840 entities. No language model proposes an entity. Tool-property annotation runs on the 72,446 72{,}446 entities in domains that can hold a physical tool. Qwen3.5-27B and gemma-4-31b each annotate every property, and each annotator’s reading is the majority over three differently worded prompts at temperature zero. Where the two disagree, both arbitrate against the written specification, and a row on which the arbiters also disagree is dropped. Most entities are not tools: the annotators reject 70,017 70{,}017 of 73,171 73{,}171 annotation rows. Screens under the same protocol check that each remaining tool acts on its axis, is deployable in the situations the template renders, and has a magnitude band. Tools mined a second time for under-supplied groups pass the same screens (orange in Figure 8 ). A last screen removes 96 96 rows whose tool is not the standard instrument of any legitimate trade (a weapon, for example), leaving 1,638 1{,}638 tool records. Pairing yields 1,422 1{,}422 tool pairs, and the grid of states over them yields 6,176 6{,}176 questions. Removing texts that collide with each other or with an evaluation set used in the paper leaves 5,751 5{,}751 . The final selection drops every situation whose questions all have the same answer: a situation recurs across tools, so its answer could otherwise be memorized. It then balances Yes and No within each remaining situation and caps any one axis, leaving the 1,880 1{,}880 questions of the main set (Table 7 ). sections.heading: A.5 Data quality
sections.text: The answer cannot be read from the wording. A lexical probe (TF-IDF features, logistic regression) is trained on the question text of some situations and read on the others. Every question of a tool that appears in the held-out situations is removed from training. Because of the state flips, such a tool would otherwise sit in training in the opposite state with the opposite answer, and the probe would learn the tool’s name with the wrong sign. The probe reaches an AUC of 0.498 ± 0.005 0.498\pm 0.005 on the main set, inside the range of 0.485 0.485 to 0.524 0.524 it reaches with permuted labels, and a lexical proxy for the answer correlates with the label at | r | = 0.022 |r|=0.022 . The set is balanced and agrees with the rule. Yes and No are exactly balanced in each of the 180 180 situations, with no imbalance per axis or per state level, and 3.9 % 3.9\% of the main set’s tool records have Yes and No counts that differ by more than one. Recomputing every answer from the annotated properties, independently of the build, gives zero mismatches, and no question text is duplicated or shared with an evaluation set used in the paper. The tool annotations, the one step where a model’s judgment enters, are reproduced by a model family that took no part in the build. GLM-4-32B re-annotated a stratified sample of 150 150 rows with the same prompts and matched the recorded value on 100 % 100\% of is-tool judgments and 92.0 % 92.0\% of axis judgments. On magnitude it placed all 150 150 tools within one band of the record, 67.3 % 67.3\% in the same band. Each of its other 49 49 judgments moves a tool from the lowest or the highest band to the middle one, so it never reverses the order of two tools by magnitude. Perturbing the annotations at this rate keeps both rankings of the models above 0.98 0.98 and moves every criterion toward acting (App. A.6 ), so annotation error does not produce the conservative criteria.

sections.heading: A.6 Robustness to annotation noise
sections.text: We test whether annotation error at the rates of App. A.5 could reorder the models or produce the conservative criteria. The perturbation acts on the magnitude band, the annotated property that sets the size of the evidence score. We hold every model’s answers fixed, perturb the magnitude of a random share of tool records, recompute the evidence score and answer of every affected question, and refit ( a , τ ) (a,\tau) , 300 300 times per condition. N1 moves 32.7 % 32.7\% of records by one band at random, the rate at which GLM-4-32B disagrees on magnitude. N2 follows its disagreement pattern, one band toward the middle. N3 scales N2 until 26 % 26\% of computed answers change, a stress level above both. A synthetic observer with each model’s fitted a a and τ = 0 \tau=0 or + 2.5 +2.5 goes through the same perturbation. Rankings are compared by Spearman correlation with the unperturbed fit, and a model’s criterion shift is the median over replicates minus its unperturbed value. sections.heading: FlipAct .
sections.text: Each question is one user turn, rendered with the model’s own chat template and its generation prompt, with no system message added. After the template’s closing “Answer Yes or No.” the prompt adds a new line, “Answer with exactly one word: Yes or No.” With reasoning off, every question of the main and supplementary sets is answered once with vLLM, sampling at temperature 0.7 0.7 , top- p p 0.8 0.8 and top- k k 20 20 with seed 0 0 and at most 8 8 new tokens, the same settings for every model except gemma-4-31b, which is run with transformers and greedy decoding. The answer is the first standalone yes or no in the output, ignoring case. An output with neither is unparsed and left out of the fit. No entry has more than one unparsed main-set question. Two further conditions guard the panel against unreadable output: at most 30 % 30\% unparsed FlipAct answers and a When2Call d ′ d^{\prime} of at least 0.5 0.5 . In practice neither removes a model that the conditions of § 4.2 admit. The fit of Eq. 2 is a maximum-likelihood logistic regression on these binary answers, so every Yes-rate and P ⁡ ( Yes ) P(\text{Yes}) on FlipAct is a proportion of sampled answers, not a token probability. SE ⁡ ( τ ) \mathrm{SE}(\tau) is half the width of the profile-likelihood interval within which the deviance rises by at most one. Nine entries were also run with seed 1 1 . The two runs give the same answer on 93 93 to 100 % 100\% of main-set questions, and for the six of the nine with a well-determined criterion both coordinates of the second run fall inside the 95 % 95\% bootstrap intervals of the first. The steering and training readouts of § 5 use the same prompt with reasoning off but do not sample: an answer is Yes when the logit of the first token of “Yes” exceeds that of “No” at the answer position.

sections.heading: Reasoning on.
sections.text: The five reasoning-on entries of Table 9 and the reasoning-on condition of App. B.7 receive the same prompt, one-word instruction included. Hybrid models reason through their template’s switch ( enable_thinking , or thinking for Granite-3.3-8B), and gpt-oss-20b runs at its template’s default reasoning effort, medium. Decoding samples at temperature 0.6 0.6 , top- p p 0.95 0.95 and top- k k 20 20 with seed 0 0 , within a budget of 8,192 8{,}192 new tokens ( 4,096 4{,}096 for Granite-3.3-8B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B). The answer is the first standalone yes or no after the end of the reasoning trace, which is the last </think> or, for gpt-oss-20b, the start of its final channel. An answer is unparsed when its trace reaches the budget without closing or is followed by no Yes or No, and no answer is read from inside a trace. A model is not fit in a mode where more than 10 % 10\% of its answers are unparsed, which removes Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B with reasoning on ( 78 % 78\% and 23 % 23\% ). Every other condition stays below 6 % 6\% , and the five reasoning-on entries of Table 9 have no unparsed answer. External benchmarks are run with reasoning off only, so reasoning-on entries have no external readout and are not in the panel.

sections.heading: External benchmarks.
sections.text: Table 11 describes the seven benchmarks. Each example is one user turn through the chat template with reasoning off, decoded greedily with vLLM (with transformers for gemma-4-31b), with at most 8 8 new tokens on QuestBench, 64 64 on When2Call, 128 128 on BFCL and 256 256 on the other four. Yes/No replies are parsed as on FlipAct . A When2Call reply is read as the letter it starts with, else a letter after a cue such as “answer” or “option” in its first 80 80 characters, else any standalone letter A–D there. On both BFCL sets a reply acts when it contains CALL: f(…) or calls a target function by name without that prefix. A reply with no parsable answer counts as withholding and stays in the denominators. No reply in the transfer test is unparsed. sections.heading: B.2 Reliability and response profile
sections.text: Both coordinates are reliable. Refitting on 200 200 random halves of the tool records with the Spearman–Brown correction gives a split-half reliability of 0.959 0.959 for a a and 0.991 0.991 for τ \tau . Tool records share question text across situations, so the stricter unit is the situation cluster, all questions that share one situation text. It is the resampling unit for every interval in the paper. Split by cluster, the two reliabilities are 0.906 0.906 and 0.973 0.973 . Models respond to the sign of the evidence score and ignore its size (Table 12 and Figure 4 ). The jump in Yes-rate between Δ ​ U = − 1 \Delta U=-1 and 0 0 is significant in 19 19 of the 21 21 models with a well-determined criterion, and the jump between 0 0 and + 1 +1 in none. Within either side, no model answers Yes reliably more often at the larger magnitude. The step therefore sits one unit below the rule’s boundary. Every question at Δ ​ U = 0 \Delta U=0 is a slight overshoot, and models accept these overshoots about as often as helpful actions: the overshoot Yes-rate lies nearer the hit rate than the false-alarm rate in most models, and its interval includes the hit rate in 20 20 of 21 21 . sections.heading: Design.
sections.text: If a model prefers one answer token whatever is asked, that preference enters its criterion (§ 4.3 ), and no single wording can separate the two. The standard probe is a balanced key ( Cronbach, 1946 ) : the same content is asked in both polarities, and one reads whether the answer follows the content or the answer word. The canonical wording closes each main-set question by asking whether using the tool is a wise choice (“wise” below). We replace that sentence with three reversed wordings, under which No means act (“Would using { t } \{t\} be an unwise choice”, “Should the person avoid using { t } \{t\} ”, “Is using { t } \{t\} a mistake”), and ask the canonical wording in the same run. Answers under a reversed wording are recoded, so every fit is P ⁡ ( act ∣ Δ ​ U ) P(\text{act}\mid\Delta U) and a model that answers the content returns the same a a and τ \tau . Five same-polarity rephrasings (appropriate, should use, right tool, makes sense, would recommend) and three answer-order variants (“Answer No or Yes”, and letter options with Yes first or with No first) check both coordinates under rewording. The run used one seed on 16 16 of the 18 18 panel models, and every rewording is compared with the canonical wording asked in the same run.

sections.heading: Decomposition.
sections.text: With both fits recoded to act polarity, write τ wise = τ d + b \tau_{\text{wise}}=\tau_{d}+b and τ unwise = τ d − b \tau_{\text{unwise}}=\tau_{d}-b . τ d \tau_{d} is a threshold on the evidence, attached to the proposition, and b b is a response bias attached to the answer word, in score units and positive when the model prefers No. Table 20 gives both as means over the three reversed wordings.

sections.heading: Criterion distillation.
sections.text: The teacher is the student itself with a steering hook. The hook adds λ ⋆ ​ w ^ ​ r ¯ / d \lambda^{\star}\hat{w}\,\bar{r}/\sqrt{d} at the 0.6 0.6 -depth layer, as in App. D.1 , but here w ^ \hat{w} is a difference of means: the mean standardized activation of the training-half questions the student answers Yes, minus that of the questions it answers No, scaled to unit norm. No labels enter it. The loss is the forward KL of Eq. 3 , with the teacher’s logits computed once on all training-half questions, and Table 26 gives the control and the optimization settings. Every criterion-distillation run of the two non-Qwen students changes MMLU by − 0.004 -0.004 to + 0.006 +0.006 . The strength comes from a FlipAct strength sweep with the same estimator. sections.heading: What the student copies.
sections.text: A teacher moved only in the criterion can be distilled because a state flip separates the two coordinates. Write ℓ + \ell_{+} and ℓ − \ell_{-} for the Yes–No logit margins on the Yes and the No question of a flip. Their difference D = ℓ + − ℓ − D=\ell_{+}-\ell_{-} measures how far apart the model holds the two states and tracks a a . Their sum Σ = ℓ + + ℓ − \Sigma=\ell_{+}+\ell_{-} measures how far both sit from zero and tracks τ \tau . A teacher moved only in τ \tau differs from the student in Σ \Sigma and not in D D . The students reproduce 0.88 0.88 to 1.04 1.04 of their teacher’s shift in Σ \Sigma . The random-direction teachers move Σ \Sigma far less than the criterion teachers, and their students’ shifts in Σ \Sigma stay small.

sections.heading: Sensitivity learning.
sections.text: The student trains answer-only on the computed answers, with the same LoRA configuration. Its pool is the training half plus supplementary questions from the same tool records (sizes and Yes share in Table 26 ). Answer-only training also breaks free-form output on Mistral-24B, so several of its external readouts, mostly on BFCL-miss-func and When2Call, cannot be scored. sections.heading: D.4 A criterion-free readout of the external benchmarks
sections.text: Distillation keeps sensitivity on a readout that carries no criterion term (§ 5.3 ). The external d ′ d^{\prime} is the equal-variance estimate from one operating point, and it is exact only when the two evidence distributions share a variance. Scoring each example of every base model, distilled student and control by its answer-token log-probability margin instead gives a full ROC and an area under it (AUC) with no criterion term. Thresholding this margin recovers the binary answers and, on the base models, the d ′ d^{\prime} and c c of the main readout. BFCL-miss-func has no answer-token margin and is absent. Distillation leaves the AUC unchanged for every student on the five benchmarks with answer log-probabilities (Table 32 ). Each distilled change is equivalent to no change under a two one-sided test at ± 0.02 \pm 0.02 , with a 90 % 90\% paired cluster-bootstrap interval inside that bound. On Qwen3-8B the change in d ′ d^{\prime} is the criterion sliding along an unequal-variance ROC. Across benchmarks the size of its criterion shift tracks the change in single-point d ′ d^{\prime} but not the change in AUC (Table 33 ). On QuestBench, where the shift is largest, d ′ d^{\prime} rises by 0.72 0.72 and the base model’s fitted ROC slope is 1.42 1.42 , against one under equal variance. sections.heading: D.6 Choosing the steering sign and strength per benchmark
sections.text: Steering with a fixed sign toward acting (the fixed push) lowers balanced accuracy on 12 12 of the 25 25 model–benchmark pairs formed by the five steered models of § 5.1 and five benchmarks (Table 36 ). The rule below, summarized in § 5.3 , instead chooses the sign and strength of the steering push from a few labeled examples of the target benchmark. The push is chosen on K = 50 K=50 labeled examples of the target benchmark, whole pairs where the benchmark has pairs, and read on the rest, over twenty random splits. On these fifty examples alone, the rule keeps the strengths at which d ′ d^{\prime} stays within a quarter of its unsteered value and takes the sign of the unsteered criterion. It pushes nothing if that criterion is smaller than its bootstrap error. Otherwise it takes the kept strength that brings c c closest to zero along a monotone path, and it pushes nothing if none qualifies. The same rule sets a scalar bias on the answer-token log-odds where the benchmark has an answer token. The readout is the change in balanced accuracy against no intervention, with a paired bootstrap over examples ( B = 2000 B=2000 ). A model–benchmark pair counts as improved when the median gain exceeds two errors and as degraded when it falls below minus one error, a stricter bar for a gain than for a loss. sections.heading: Appendix E A model that returns a probability
sections.text: Every entry in the paper is a token model read through a Yes/No answer, so its criterion can include a preference for one answer word (§ 4.3 ). JEV ( TypeSafe AI, 2026 ) is a decision model of a different kind. 3 3 3 Model jev-latest , API version jev-1.13.0 , evaluated 2026-09-22. Given a state and a statement about it, JEV returns the probability that the statement is true and generates no text, so it gives a readout of FlipAct with no answer word to prefer. The state is a question’s situation and action sentences, and the statement is “Using the tool is a wise choice in this situation”. The returned probability is read as P ⁡ ( act ) P(\text{act}) and binarized at one half for the fit of Eq. 2 . Because this input differs from the prompt the token models receive, JEV is not entered in Figure 5 , the panel or Table 9 , and the comparisons below are descriptive.

sections.heading: Coordinates.
sections.text: On the statement readout JEV has a = 0.62 a=0.62 and τ = + 1.35 \tau=+1.35 (Table 38 ). Its sensitivity is close to that of the most sensitive entries of Table 9 . The criterion is conservative, with an interval that excludes zero, and lies between those of Llama-3.3-70B and gemma-4-31b. Mean P ⁡ ( act ) P(\text{act}) steps between Δ ​ U = − 1 \Delta U=-1 and 0 0 and is flat on either side, the same profile as the token models in Figure 4 . Asked instead to rate, on an ordered verbal scale, the action’s effect on the situation or how warranted it is, JEV tracks the size of the evidence barely better than its probability does. When the statement is reversed, JEV’s answer preference in the decomposition of App. C is b = − 0.20 ± 0.24 b=-0.20\pm 0.24 , and the probabilities under the two polarities sum to 1.01 1.01 on average.

sections.heading: Readout format.
sections.text: Asked to choose between use and avoid instead of judging the statement, JEV returns the same coordinates (Table 38 ), so on FlipAct its criterion does not depend on how the binary decision is read out. It does depend on which decisions are offered. On When2Call, where many withhold examples call for asking a question, JEV has c = − 1.15 c=-1.15 when it judges a statement. Offered a choice among call, ask and decline, it routes most of those examples to ask, and c c moves to + 0.02 +0.02 . A criterion read from two options is therefore not a constant of the model when a third option exists, which is one reason an absolute τ \tau need not predict a benchmark’s c c . sections.heading: Caveats.
sections.text: JEV is one closed model under one API version, and its responses are deterministic, so every interval resamples situations or examples only. Binarizing its probability also adds a threshold the token models do not have. JEV shows that a conservative criterion and a step at the sign of the evidence can arise without an answer word, but a single model cannot stand in for the 44 44 models.

sections.heading: Appendix F When-to-act benchmarks, steering and efficient inference
sections.text: Table 39 places twelve when-to-act benchmarks on the design choices of § 2 : how the ground truth is constructed, whether controlled negatives are matched, whether the evidence for acting is graded, and whether responses are decomposed into sensitivity and criterion. The decisions cover tool-call necessity ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Patil et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , acting or abstaining on minimally perturbed pairs ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , answering or abstaining ( Kirichenko et al., 2026 ) , clarification ( Li et al., 2026 ; Su and Cardie, 2026 ) , over-refusal ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) and physical affordance ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) . Activation steering reads a direction from the residual stream and adds it back ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2023 ; Turner et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . Refusal is its best-studied target ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , and sycophancy is a related disposition ( Sharma et al., 2024 ; Perez et al., 2023 ) . App. D.1 projects the refusal and sycophancy directions out of the criterion direction as a control on the steering result. The decision to act also appears inside efficient inference, where the action is to spend more computation. LoHi ( Dong et al., 2026c ) answers from a low-resolution video stream first and requests high-resolution frames only when the entropy of the answer exceeds a threshold, which sends about a third of the questions to the second pass at nearly the accuracy of always requesting them; the threshold is a criterion in the sense used here. MMTok ( Dong et al., 2026b ) observes that the number of visual tokens a question needs depends on its difficulty, and MAI ( Dong et al., 2026a ) passes a small model’s reasoning to a large one only when needed. The last of these also shows the failure this paper measures: asked whether a fan suits a user who feels cold, a small vision-language model states that a fan cools and still answers that it is suitable. sections.heading: Instrument.
sections.text: Every label is computed by rule from a tool’s direction and magnitude on one axis, annotated by language models with no person in the loop, so some questions will carry labels a person would set otherwise. Agreement between annotator families and perturbations of the annotations check how far such errors could move the results (App. A.5 and A.6 ); no human observers were measured on the diagnostic. All questions share one template in one physical domain. The criterion stays positive in nearly all models under five rephrasings of it (App. C ); other templates and domains are untested. Side effects, annotated for part of the tool records, do not enter the rule.

sections.heading: Measurement.
sections.text: Several relations rest on few models. The fall of the criterion with size inside a family rests on three to five models per family. The FlipAct criterion does not track a benchmark’s c c consistently: near zero on three benchmarks, positive on BFCL on the strength of the three models with the lowest τ \tau , and negative on When2Call at a looser panel cutoff (Table 15 , App. B.4 ), over eighteen models whose criteria sit in a narrow band. Whether this comes from limited power, from the benchmarks’ interfaces or from the construct is open. All models are open checkpoints of at most 70 70 B parameters.

sections.heading: Interventions.
sections.text: Two of the intervention models, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-27B, answer No under either wording, so part of their starting τ \tau is a preference for the answer token (App. C ). The steering direction depends on the wording it is read under, so the interventions are read from behavior, not from the geometry of the direction (App. D.1 ). After distillation the equivalence test on sensitivity is undecided on Qwen3-8B and Mistral-24B. The Yes-bias comparison covers two students, with BFCL-miss-func as its only free-form test (App. D.5 ). The reasoning-mode comparison rests mostly on Qwen models. Sensitivity learning raises a a on FlipAct but does not transfer stably to the external benchmarks: its changes in d ′ d^{\prime} and c c there differ in sign across students and are matched by the shuffled-label control. FlipAct tests basic physical knowledge of tools, and labels on it appear to add little that sharpens the decision to call a tool elsewhere.

sections.heading: Outlook.
sections.text: The build scales with annotator calls (§ 3.4 ), and its schema is written in a domain-specific language ( Chen et al., 2026 ) in which a property, an axis or a rule can be added or removed without rebuilding the pipeline. Richer tool properties such as side effects, rules over several properties and their interactions ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and new axes, templates and domains run through the same steps. Beyond single decisions, a richer graph of how tools transform states could chain questions into multi-step agent scenarios, in which a model’s tendencies can be read across a sequence of decisions. Such scenarios may also supply what sensitivity learning needs to transfer beyond FlipAct .

Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act Sixun Dong Affiliation: University of Central Florida Email: sixundong@ucf.edu Yebowen Hu Affiliation: Zoom Communications Email: yebowen.hu@zoom.us Ming Yin Affiliation: Duke University Email: chen.chen@crcv.ucf.edu Yiran Chen Affiliation: Duke University Fei Liu Affiliation: Emory University Chen Chen Affiliation: University of Central Florida Abstract Before an agent acts it must decide whether any action is warranted. Benchmarks that ask this question report one accuracy, which cannot distinguish a model that fails to recognize a warranted action from one that recognizes it but is reluctant to act. Signal-detection theory separates the two as sensitivity and criterion, but a criterion estimated from authored binary labels depends on each benchmark’s mix of examples and cannot be compared across benchmarks. We introduce FlipAct , a diagnostic built on a qualitative representation of what tools do to physical states. A rule over annotated tool properties computes each question’s answer and a graded evidence score, with the Yes/No boundary fixed at zero for every model, so every answer is computed, not written by a model. Questions are built from 2 × 2 2\times 2 quads that hold the required knowledge fixed while the state flips. The slope of a model’s Yes-rate against the score is its sensitivity, and the score where it crosses one half is its criterion. Across 44 44 open models, sensitivity rises with size within a family, and its ranking agrees with three of four external when-to-act benchmarks. Models respond to the sign of the evidence rather than its size, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, most models are conservative and stay so when the question is rephrased. In some models this is a preference for answering No, and the criterion is not set by size. Activation steering moves the criterion with the weights fixed, and distilling a model from its own steered copy moves it in the weights, without a significant change in sensitivity. The distilled shift carries to six external benchmarks with sensitivity kept, including two without a Yes/No answer. Accuracy rises where the model started conservative and falls where it started permissive. Project page: https://sixundong.com/projects/flipact . † † footnotetext: 🖂 Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents must decide whether to act before they decide how. Benchmarks for agents mostly score the action once taken: whether the chosen function, its arguments and the trajectory are correct ( Patil et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2026 ) . Those that study the decision itself, in tool calling ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) , clarification ( Li et al., 2026 ) and abstention ( Kirichenko et al., 2026 ) , report a single accuracy, and that number mixes two ways to fail. A model may not recognize whether a situation warrants action, a failure of its sensitivity ; or it may recognize the situation and still be too reluctant or too ready to act, a failure of its criterion . Too conservative a criterion refuses benign requests ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) or answers from memory where a tool was needed; too permissive a criterion acts where nothing warrants it. On When2Call ( Ross et al., 2025 ) , gemma-2-9b and Phi-3.5-mini reach balanced accuracies of 0.65 0.65 and 0.64 0.64 with opposite behavior: the first rarely calls the tool, even where it should, and the second calls it on most examples, many where it should not (Figure 1 a). They separate the two kinds of example about equally well, so on this benchmark the first should act more and the second less. Signal-detection theory ( Green et al., 1966 ) separates sensitivity ( d ′ d^{\prime} ) from criterion (Figure 1 b; § 3.1 ), but on a benchmark with binary labels the criterion it recovers is relative to that benchmark’s mix of examples, and no zero is shared across benchmarks. Comparing criteria needs a fixed boundary on a common evidence scale, which authored binary labels do not provide ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 , cf.) . 0 0.5 1 call rate .40 .10 .86 .58 gemma-2-9b bal. acc. .65 Phi-3.5-mini bal. acc. .64 should call should not (a) Same accuracy, opposite calls unwarranted warranted Phi-3.5-mini’s criterion gemma-2-9b’s criterion evidence for acting → \rightarrow same d ′ d^{\prime} (b) Same d ′ d^{\prime} , two criteria No ( Δ ​ U ≤ 0 \Delta U\leq 0 ) Yes ( Δ ​ U > 0 \Delta U>0 ) Δ ​ U \Delta U − 3 -3 − 2 -2 − 1 -1 0 0 1 1 2 2 3 3 dehumid. dry humid. wet humid. dry dehumid. wet (c) Evidence computed by rule Figure 1: (a) Share of should-call and of should-not-call When2Call examples that each model calls. (b) Schematic: at one sensitivity d ′ d^{\prime} , the two models’ criteria trade hits for false alarms at the same accuracy. (c) The quad of Figure 2 on the evidence scale Δ ​ U \Delta U that FlipAct computes by rule, with the Yes/No boundary fixed at zero. FlipAct supplies such a scale by computing the evidence for acting. Its design draws on qualitative process theory ( Forbus, 1984 ) , which describes physical change by the sign of each quantity’s change and a coarse ordinal magnitude, enough to say what an action does to a state without numbers. Each question shows a situation and a candidate tool and asks whether using the tool is warranted. The state and the tool each have a sign and an ordinal magnitude on a physical axis. A rule over these properties computes the evidence score Δ ​ U \Delta U , how much closer the action brings the state to its goal, with the Yes/No boundary at zero (Figure 1 c). The design unit is a 2 × 2 2\times 2 quad : two tools, each shown in the state it fixes and in the state it worsens, so the knowledge needed to answer stays the same and the state decides the answer (Figure 2 ). Fitting a model’s Yes-rate against Δ ​ U \Delta U gives its sensitivity as the slope a a and its criterion as the score τ \tau where it crosses one half. Across 44 44 open models (§ 4 ), sensitivity behaves as expected of a capability: it rises with size inside a family, and its ranking agrees with external d ′ d^{\prime} on three of four when-to-act benchmarks. Models read the sign of the evidence rather than its size, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, the criterion is mostly conservative, in some models through a preference for answering No. It is a stable per-model setting, not set by size: two releases of Mistral-Small-24B sit on opposite sides of zero. We move the criterion separately from sensitivity in two ways (§ 5 ). At inference, adding a direction read from the model’s own activations ( Zou et al., 2023 ; Turner et al., 2023 ; Ke et al., 2026 ) shifts the criterion with the weights fixed. In the weights, distilling the model from its own steered copy shifts the criterion on four models from three developers with no significant change in sensitivity, and a random direction of the same norm does not. The shift carries beyond FlipAct ’s Yes/No format: on benchmarks without a Yes/No answer it exceeds the shift from a teacher that only favors Yes, on both models tested. On every benchmark, accuracy rises or falls as the starting criterion predicts. Supervised training on the computed labels instead raises sensitivity and moves the criterion with it. Contributions. 1. A measurement scheme that splits when-to-act accuracy into a sensitivity and a criterion, read against an evidence scale computed by rule with the Yes/No boundary fixed for every model. 2. FlipAct , built by an automated pipeline in which language models only annotate what a tool does, while the states and every answer follow from the rule. 3. Evidence that the criterion moves separately from sensitivity: steering and distillation from a steered copy move the criterion, while training on the computed labels raises sensitivity. 2 Related work When-to-act evaluation. Benchmarks for deciding whether to act cover tool calling ( Ross et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Patil et al., 2025 ) , clarification ( Li et al., 2026 ) , abstention ( Kirichenko et al., 2026 ) and over-refusal ( Röttger et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Most share three design choices: ground truth is authored by humans or an LLM judge, the evidence for acting is a binary label, and performance is a single rate that conflates a model’s sensitivity with its criterion. Li et al. (2026) instead compute ground truth by constraint satisfaction, and Sun et al. (2026) fix a controlled call/no-call boundary with deliberate no-tool cases. Neither flips a world-state while holding the required knowledge fixed, and none of these benchmarks grades the evidence for acting per question. We reuse four of them as external tests (§ 4.2 ) and measure transfer on six benchmarks (§ 5.3 ). App. F compares twelve on these design choices. Signal detection and language models. Signal-detection theory separates an observer’s sensitivity from its criterion ( Green et al., 1966 ) . Reading a benchmark score as the measurement of a latent quantity raises the question of whether it measures what it is read as ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 ; Bean et al., 2026 ) . Cacioli (2026) fits signal-detection models to factual question answering with the model’s answer log-probability as evidence, so the criterion sits on each model’s own confidence scale. Shi et al. (2026) read a call/no-call offset off sparse-autoencoder features on When2Call and cancel it by steering. Their offset is an intercept on an internal margin, compared within one model and without a separate sensitivity. FlipAct places the criterion on a rule-computed evidence scale shared across questions and models, estimates it separately from sensitivity with the required knowledge held fixed, and moves it into the weights. 3 The FlipAct diagnostic 3.1 Preliminaries: signal detection Signal-detection theory ( Green et al., 1966 ) models an observer who reports a signal whenever a scalar amount of evidence exceeds a threshold. The sensitivity d ′ d^{\prime} is the distance between the evidence distributions of signal and noise trials in units of their spread, and the criterion c c is where the threshold sits relative to their midpoint. From the hit rate H H and the false-alarm rate FA \mathrm{FA} the equal-variance estimators, with z z the inverse of the standard normal distribution function, are d ′ = z ⁡ ( H ) − z ⁡ ( FA ) , c = − 1 2 ​ ( z ⁡ ( H ) + z ⁡ ( FA ) ) . d^{\prime}\;=\;z(H)-z(\mathrm{FA}),\qquad c\;=\;-\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(z(H)+z(\mathrm{FA})\bigr). (1) In when-to-act terms a hit is acting when one should and a false alarm is acting when one should not. A positive c c is conservative. FlipAct supplies an evidence score per question, and the same two quantities become the slope a a and the crossing point τ \tau of a model’s Yes-rate against that score (§ 4.1 ). Every comparison in the paper pairs a a with d ′ d^{\prime} and τ \tau with c c . Each question shows a physical situation, the goal of returning it to normal and one candidate tool, and asks whether using the tool is a wise choice. All questions share one minimal template (Figure 2 ), as do the stimuli of template-based diagnostics ( McCoy et al., 2019 ; Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) , so only the tool, the state and their outcome vary. Physical situations are used because a tool’s effect on a state can be written as an explicit qualitative transition: a humidifier helps a dry room and harms a wet one. In the quad of Figure 2 , a humidifier that adds two steps of moisture and an industrial dehumidifier that removes three are crossed with a very dry and a dangerously wet room. Every question of the quad needs the same two facts, what the tool does and what the room needs. For a given tool only the state changes, and with it the answer, so a model that knows what a humidifier is for must still read the state. Quads and state flips are controls built into the set. The main set has 1,880 1{,}880 questions: 840 840 lie in a complete quad and 1,256 1{,}256 belong to a state flip , the same tool with opposite answers in two states. A state flip separates a model that ignores the state, which gives both questions about the same Yes–No logit margin, from one that is merely permissive, which may answer Yes to both but still ranks the warranted one higher (App. D.3 , D.7 ). Every situation has as many Yes as No questions, so the description of the world does not predict the answer. 3.3 Ground truth and evidence by rule Each situation fixes an integer state v v on a physical axis (thermal transfer, moisture, mechanical cohesion, …) with the goal at 0 0 . Each tool carries a direction δ ∈ { + 1 , − 1 } \delta\in\{+1,-1\} and an ordinal magnitude band μ ∈ { 1 , 2 , 3 } \mu\in\{1,2,3\} on that axis ( Forbus, 1984 , in qualitative process theory, a sign and a place in a quantity space;) , optionally conditional on a prerequisite. Applying it moves the state to v + δ ​ μ v+\delta\mu , and the process behind that change is not modeled. The evidence score is the utility of the action, how much closer to the goal it leaves the world, Δ ​ U = | v | − | v + δ ​ μ | , Yes ⇔ Δ ​ U > 0 , \Delta U\;=\;|v|\;-\;|v+\delta\mu|,\qquad\texttt{Yes}\iff\Delta U>0, and a tool with unmet prerequisites carries Δ ​ U = − 2 \Delta U=-2 for each, a value set by convention. The question type follows from the same computation: a wrong-direction tool is destructive , a right-direction tool that overshoots or acts on a state already at the goal is redundant , and a tool applied without its prerequisite is prerequisite . Because v v and μ \mu are integers, Δ ​ U \Delta U takes seven values on [ − 3 , 3 ] [-3,3] . A question conveys | v | |v| only by the adverb slightly , very or dangerously , and μ \mu only by the tool itself. Language models annotate each tool’s axis, direction, magnitude and prerequisite, and the rule computes the answer from those properties. 3.4 An automated build FlipAct is generated by a pipeline (Figure 3 ) that needs no per-question human annotation or adjudication. Its specification is written once: the physical axes, a closed vocabulary of tool properties, the rule of § 3.3 and the template. Ten lexical, medical and visually grounded resources supply 149,840 149{,}840 candidate entities, and two annotator models, Qwen3.5-27B and gemma-4-31b, fill the vocabulary for each. Where they disagree, both arbitrate against the specification, and unresolved records are dropped. Tool records (one tool, one axis) are paired when they act in opposite directions on that axis and target object, and states, answers, question types and text follow by rule. A balance selection keeps 1,880 1{,}880 of the 6,176 6{,}176 rendered questions. Limitations are discussed in App. G . 6 Conclusion We treated the decision to act as a measurement problem. Two models with the same accuracy can need opposite fixes, so a when-to-act benchmark says more when it reports d ′ d^{\prime} and c c beside accuracy. The criterion moves, at inference or in the weights, with a shift whose sign the target benchmark sets, while sensitivity on FlipAct rises with training on labels. On a Yes/No format the criterion also holds a preference between answer words, which reversed wordings separate from the rest.
